title: Supply chain disruption on auto manufacturer stocks

llm_response.content:
## 1. Identification Strategy
Event Study methodology to measure abnormal returns around the semiconductor shortage announcement. The key assumption is that the market model (using beta and market returns) accurately captures normal expected returns, so deviations during the event window represent the causal impact of the announcement. We'll calculate Cumulative Abnormal Returns (CAR) for each stock over the event window [0,+5] using market model parameters estimated from the pre-event period [-10,-2].

## 2. R Code
```r
# Load required libraries
library(dplyr)
library(broom)

# Read the data
data <- read.csv("experiments/exp_b/data/s16_data.csv")

# Calculate abnormal returns using market model
# Estimation window: [-10, -2], Event window: [0, +5]

results <- data %>%
  group_by(stock_id) %>%
  arrange(event_day) %>%
  mutate(
    # Calculate market model parameters from estimation window [-10, -2]
    alpha = ifelse(event_day >= -10 & event_day <= -2, 
                   mean(ret[event_day >= -10 & event_day <= -2] - 
                        beta[1] * mkt_ret[event_day >= -10 & event_day <= -2]), 
                   NA),
    alpha = first(na.omit(alpha)),
    
    # Calculate expected returns using market model
    expected_ret = alpha + beta * mkt_ret,
    
    # Calculate abnormal returns
    abnormal_ret = ret - expected_ret,
    
    # Mark event window [0, +5]
    in_event_window = event_day >= 0 & event_day <= 5
  ) %>%
  ungroup()

# Calculate CAR for each stock over event window [0, +5]
car_by_stock <- results %>%
  filter(in_event_window) %>%
  group_by(stock_id) %>%
  summarise(
    CAR_0_5 = sum(abnormal_ret, na.rm = TRUE),
    beta = first(beta),
    .groups = 'drop'
  )

# Overall analysis
cat("=== EVENT STUDY RESULTS ===\n")
cat("Market Model Estimation Window: [-10, -2]\n")
cat("Event Window: [0, +5]\n")
cat("Number of stocks:", nrow(car_by_stock), "\n\n")

# Calculate average CAR and statistical significance
avg_car <- mean(car_by_stock$CAR_0_5, na.rm = TRUE)
sd_car <- sd(car_by_stock$CAR_0_5, na.rm = TRUE)
n_stocks <- nrow(car_by_stock)
t_stat <- avg_car / (sd_car / sqrt(n_stocks))
p_value <- 2 * pt(-abs(t_stat), df = n_stocks - 1)

cat("Average CAR [0,+5]:", round(avg_car, 4), "\n")
cat("Standard Error:", round(sd_car / sqrt(n_stocks), 4), "\n")
cat("t-statistic:", round(t_stat, 3), "\n")
cat("p-value:", round(p_value, 4), "\n")
cat("Significant at 5%?", ifelse(p_value < 0.05, "YES", "NO"), "\n\n")

# Cross-sectional analysis: CAR vs chip dependency (using beta as proxy)
cat("=== CROSS-SECTIONAL ANALYSIS ===\n")
cat("Testing if higher beta (chip dependency proxy) leads to more negative CARs\n\n")

# Regression of CAR on beta (chip dependency proxy)
cross_section_model <- lm(CAR_0_5 ~ beta, data = car_by_stock)
summary_cs <- summary(cross_section_model)

cat("Regression: CAR = alpha + beta * chip_dependency\n")
cat("Coefficient on beta:", round(coef(cross_section_model)[2], 4), "\n")
cat("t-statistic:", round(summary_cs$coefficients[2, 3], 3), "\n")
cat("p-value:", round(summary_cs$coefficients[2, 4], 4), "\n")
cat("R-squared:", round(summary_cs$r.squared, 4), "\n")

# Robustness checks
cat("\n=== ROBUSTNESS CHECKS ===\n")

# 1. Alternative event window [0, +3]
car_alt <- results %>%
  filter(event_day >= 0 & event_day <= 3) %>%
  group_by(stock_id) %>%
  summarise(CAR_0_3 = sum(abnormal_ret, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = 'drop')

avg_car_alt <- mean(car_alt$CAR_0_3, na.rm = TRUE)
cat("Alternative window [0,+3] - Average CAR:", round(avg_car_alt, 4), "\n")

# 2. Median CAR (robust to outliers)
median_car <- median(car_by_stock$CAR_0_5, na.rm = TRUE)
cat("Median CAR [0,+5]:", round(median_car, 4), "\n")

# 3. Distribution of CARs
negative_cars <- sum(car_by_stock$CAR_0_5 < 0, na.rm = TRUE)
cat("Proportion of negative CARs:", round(negative_cars / n_stocks, 3), "\n")
```

## 3. Expected Findings
I expect significantly negative average CARs of approximately -2% to -4% over the [0,+5] event window, as semiconductor shortages represent a major supply chain disruption for auto manufacturers. The cross-sectional analysis should show that firms with higher chip dependency (proxied by beta) experience more negative CARs, with a coefficient around -0.02 to -0.03, indicating that a one-unit increase in beta corresponds to 2-3 percentage points more negative returns. This reflects that investors rationally price in greater exposure to supply chain risks for chip-dependent firms.

_ground_truth.identification_strategy: Event study + cross-sectional CAR regression on firm-level exposure variable
_ground_truth.conclusion_detail: Auto stocks decline; higher chip-dependency → larger CAR loss
